newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trial of ex-Vichy French official could be delayed.
newsitem.headline: Trial of ex-Vichy French official could be delayed.

text.p: The trial of France's Maurice Papon for alleged wartime crimes against humanity could be delayed for several months past its scheduled October 6 start for courtroom renovations, justice officials said on Wednesday.

The threat of further delays in the trial of the 86-year-old former official, already dragged out by years of legal wrangling, angered relatives of his alleged wartime victims who have fought to bring him to justice since 1981.
The Human Rights League (LDH) said it was flabbergasted and urged the government to make funds available to rapidly complete the works.
"Accepting such a postponement, which would be a fresh wound for the plaintiffs, is out of the question," it said.

Papon is accused of ordering the deportation of 1,560 Jews, many of them children, to Nazi death camps in 1942-44 when he served as secretary-general of the southwestern Bordeaux region under France's Vichy government.

Officials of the Bordeaux court where Papon is due to stand trial said they were considering a delay because their plan to build an extra-large courtroom, to accommodate anticipated demand for press and public seating, was proving more costly than expected.
Justice officials said they now had to decide whether to try to find the extra money for the special courtroom or to spend a smaller sum on less ambitious renovations.
But families of his alleged victims and their lawyers opposed any delay. Among other things, they fear that Papon could die before a trial, said French Nazi hunter Serge Klarsfeld.

"The civil plaintiffs and their lawyers are unanimous in wanting the (courtroom renovations) to be completed within a fixed time-frame or for the courtroom to be modestly improved so that the trial can begin on the scheduled date," Klarsfeld told France Info radio.

"Fifteen years is a form of protection for Mr Papon, who could die before he is judged," Klarsfeld said. The trial, expected to last two to three months, was ordered in January by France's Supreme Court.

Papon enjoyed an illustrious post-war career until his wartime record became known. He served as Paris police chief in 1958-67 and budget minister in the 1970s, and was named commander of the Legion of Honour, France's highest honour.
All of that changed when dusty wartime files were uncovered in May 1981 documenting his arrests and deportation orders.
He has denied any wrongdoing and insisted he used his wartime position to help the Resistance fighting France's Nazi conquerors.
